{"self_assessment": "Impact: I laid the upper tail, which is the piece that gives the fish its forked tail and makes the outline read as a fish at a glance. I made the join at the crossing where the body lines meet the tail, so the fall carries from the body into the tail. When the first upper tail came out jammed, I lifted it and laid it again. The relaid piece fell dark most of the way round to the fork. Near the end I lifted a stray at the top right of the tail so those dominoes went back to the pile for Maya's last joins. The table's run covered about 199 of 248 standing dominoes when I last traced it by eye.

Execution: I stayed in my lane, which was the upper tail and the joins between pieces, and I did not redo other people's strokes. I spotted early that the start's run wasn't reaching the top line and worked on the nose with Priya until the fall climbed into it. I checked the tail tip and the notch and reported what I found. I also checked the crossing and nudged a domino there that sat off line.

Collaboration: I kept my updates short and specific so others knew what I was touching. I asked Leo to check the tip from his side. When Maya took the notch join I stepped off so we wouldn't bump each other. I also kept clear of that area, and my spare dominoes helped her finish.

Leadership: I didn't set the plan, since Priya did. I led by taking ownership of the upper tail and the joins and by flagging the nose problem early. I also kept the table's attention on what was still open, the notch, rather than on finished work.

My honest estimate is that I did roughly a fifth of the table's result. Priya drew the plan and the top line, Maya the bottom line and the notch joins, and Leo the lower tail and body joins.", "my_share_percent": 20}
